title: Shortcut Bench
context: Grade 4, and the chapter stops calculating here to ask what may be changed without spoiling the answer. An adult sees five properties and a handful of shortcuts. What the page is actually doing is showing that the shortcuts are the properties being used on purpose: multiplying by a multiple of ten is the expanding rule, and pairing two of three numbers to make a round number is the grouping rule. A child who meets them as separate tricks has six things to remember instead of two.

writeup.why: Find out what you are allowed to change about a multiplication without changing its answer, and let the zeros of a round number do the work.
writeup.look: Two trays side by side sharing one set of number cards, an expand and add strip below them and a rail of opening zeros along the foot.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Shortcut Bench' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the arrangements worked against the arrangements standing on the bench, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each tray lands a product and the second fixed at what the bench is holding. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. Two trays stand across the top of the working area, each 500 by 200, the left at 64,202 and the right at 650,202, with a still gap of 86 between them that never holds anything. One set of number cards belongs to both trays: a card is 132 by 96, drawn as a solid plate with its number large, and the same card can stand in either tray. A swap control under a tray reverses the cards in it. Brackets are drawn as two heavy curves that close around any pair in a three card tray, and the bracketed pair is then worked first and held afterwards as one card with its own number on it. A one card and a zero card sit on the bench corner at 1020,158 and can be dropped into either tray at any time, the tray handing the long number straight back for the one and collapsing visibly to nothing for the zero. Both trays work at once and their products land together on a shared ledge under the gap, side by side and level, and under each product its own working is drawn out in full so that the two pieces of working can be read against one another as well as the two answers. The expand and add strip opens beneath the trays, 1086 by 132 at 64,428: it writes the multiplicand as its hundreds, tens and ones with plus signs 28 tall between them, gives each part its own small row and its own product, and adds those rows back, with the whole number worked alongside in a column of its own. The zeros rail runs along the foot, 1086 by 108 at 64,592: the number sits on it with closed places drawn to its right, and multiplying by ten, a hundred or a thousand opens one, two or three of them, the digits sliding left as the places open and every place naming itself as it fills, the opening zeros drawn grey because they are holding places and not counting anything. For a multiple such as sixty or eight hundred the short fact is worked above the rail first and only then are the multiplier's own zeros opened. The pairing bay sits at the right of the rail, 320 by 108, taking three cards and, once the child has chosen, lighting whichever two of them multiply to a round number. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a product or a part of one is asked for, and on the second and fourth phases a choice pad holding the arrangements themselves, so that an order or a pair can be picked with one press instead of typed out. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the number being multiplied is deep blue, the number it is multiplied by is amber, and the product standing under the rule is green; a digit carried into the next column is vermilion and is always drawn small and inside a ring set above the column it is joining, never in the margin and never under the rule; a partial product row made by one place of the multiplier is rose; and a zero that is only holding a place open, or a step that is skipped, is grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and every one of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a column is told by the heading written above it before it is ever told by a colour, and a carried digit by being small and by sitting in a ring above the column it is going into.
writeup.finish: The card shows one product worked two ways with its answers together, and the number from the zeros rail with its places still open.

phases.win: the first tray hands the number back unchanged and the second collapses to nothing
phases.does: drops each card in turn and reads what came back
phases.goal: a product with one gives the number back and a product with zero gives nothing
phases.says: Take the number once. Now take it no times at all. What came back each time?
phases.check: What is 56,902 x 1, and what is 9,63,201 x 0?
phases.feels: two cards that need no working at all, whatever number happens to be in the tray
phases.hands: On paper write any number you like and multiply it by one, then by zero. Do it again with a number long enough to fill the line, and again with a number only two digits long. Ask whether the length of the number made any difference to either of the two answers.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many times is the number in the tray being taken? Second rung, the phase's: what is left when a number is taken no times at all? Third rung: the tray is cut to a two digit number and the child drops each of the two cards into it in turn. The choice pad stays open behind all three.

wrong.why: one and zero both look like small quiet numbers that leave things alone, and a child who has just watched one hand a number back expects the next small card to do something of the same kind.
wrong.move: gives the number itself as the answer to the zero, by treating zero the way one had just behaved.
wrong.screen: the tray holding the number is emptied slowly out onto the bench as equal groups, and then the zero card asks for that many groups to be taken: the bench counts out no groups at all and stands bare, with the child's answer left in the slot beside the empty bench and nothing marked.

wrong.why: two odd little cards offered together look like two halves of one rule, and the rule that was just heard was about nothing being left.
wrong.move: answers zero for the product with one as well, because the two cards were dropped into the tray in the same breath.
wrong.screen: the two cards separate and are worked in two rows one above the other, each with a tray of its own: the one row hands the long number back digit for digit with the two readings stood together and matching, and the zero row collapses to nothing. Neither row is cleared while the other runs.

phases.screen: a tray holding one long number, with a one card and a zero card waiting beside it
phases.soWhat: Multiplying by one gives the number back unchanged, and multiplying by zero gives zero.
phases.concept: One leaves it alone and zero flattens it

phases.win: both trays land on the same product and the pairing bay lights the pair that makes a round number
phases.does: works both trays and reads the two products against each other
phases.goal: swapping the cards, or bracketing a different pair, leaves the product alone
phases.says: Swap them over, then work both trays. Did the product move?
phases.check: 512 x 2 comes to 1024. Without multiplying anything, what does 2 x 512 come to, and does its working have to look the same?
phases.feels: the arrangement is a free choice, and the answer does not care which choice was made
phases.hands: Write one multiplication on paper and work it in full. Then write the same two numbers with their positions swapped and work that in full as well. Hold the two answers together, then hold the two pieces of working together, and ask which of the two they would rather have had to write out.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which cards are standing in the tray? Second rung, the phase's: what does changing their order do to the product? Third rung: both trays are cut to two small cards each and the child works the two arrangements by hand. The choice pad stays open.

wrong.why: a rule has just been heard, and a rule heard is a reason to stop working; copying across is what a rule of that kind seems to be for.
wrong.move: works only the left tray and copies its answer into the right one, because the cards are the same and the answer is bound to be.
wrong.screen: the right tray works its own arrangement anyway, slowly, every step drawn where the child could have drawn it, and the two products land side by side on the ledge and match. The two pieces of working are then stood one above the other, where they are plainly not the same shape, with the rows of each counted along the margin. The copied answer is left exactly where it was put and nothing is marked.

wrong.why: a bench of loose cards invites everything on it to be rearranged, and the rule that was just given said the arrangement was a free choice.
wrong.move: changes one of the cards as well as the order, because swapping and rewriting feel like the same tidying up.
wrong.screen: the changed card is drawn back to the bench edge and the card it replaced returns to its tray, and both trays are then worked on the cards they share. The product the changed card would have given is worked in a third small row beneath the ledge and stood beside the other two, where it does not match either of them.

phases.screen: the same cards in both trays, arranged differently in each
phases.soWhat: Swapping the two numbers, or bracketing a different pair, leaves the product alone, so pick the arrangement you would rather work.
phases.concept: The order is yours to choose

phases.win: the parts add to the same product the whole number gave, standing beside it
phases.does: multiplies each part in its own row, then adds the rows up
phases.goal: a multiplicand split by place gives parts that multiply separately and add back
phases.says: Break it into its places. Multiply each piece. Now put the pieces back together.
phases.check: Which of these is another way to find 65 x 7: (60 x 7) + (5 x 7), or (60 + 7) x (5 + 7)?
phases.feels: the pieces are small enough to do in the head, and they still add back to the whole thing
phases.hands: Write 625 on paper as 600 + 20 + 5, multiply each part by 5 in its own line, and add the three lines up. Then work 625 x 5 in columns beside it. Ask which of the two they could have done without writing anything down at all.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what are the places of the number being broken up? Second rung, the phase's: what has to happen to every one of those parts? Third rung: the strip is cut to a two digit number split into its tens and its ones, and the child works both small rows and adds them. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the hundreds part is worth far more than the other two put together, and an answer that is nearly right feels like an answer that is finished.
wrong.move: multiplies the hundreds part, stops there, and reads that as the answer.
wrong.screen: the two parts that were never taken stay on the strip drawn grey with their small rows left empty and ringed, and the total the child gave is stood against the total of all three rows, with the gap between them written out beside it as the two parts that were left behind: 3000 given, 3125 wanted, and 100 and 25 never taken.

wrong.why: once the multiplicand has been split, splitting the other number looks like the same move made twice, and two rows of parts standing level with each other invite being read straight across.
wrong.move: breaks the multiplier into parts as well, pairs each part off with the part standing level with it, and adds just those products.
wrong.screen: a line is drawn from every part of the one number to every part of the other, so the pairings the child never made show up as lines with nothing written on them; the strip then closes the multiplier back into a single card and each part of the multiplicand is taken by the whole of it in turn. The child's rows stay on the bench while both readings are worked.

phases.screen: the expand and add strip with the multiplicand broken into its hundreds, tens and ones
phases.soWhat: Break the multiplicand into its places, multiply every one of those places, and add the parts.
phases.concept: A number can be broken up before it is multiplied

phases.win: the digits stay put, the zeros open beneath them and the rail names the places they fill
phases.does: multiplies by ten, then by a hundred, then by a multiple, counting the zeros each time
phases.goal: a round multiplier is handled by a short fact and the zeros it carries
phases.says: Say how many zeros will follow before you press. Then press and count them.
phases.check: 58 x 7 = 406. What is 58 x 7000, and how many zeros did the multiplier carry?
phases.feels: the digits stay exactly as they were and the only thing that changes is how many places have opened under them
phases.hands: On paper write 398 x 6, and under it write 398 x 60. Work the first, then look hard at the second before working it. Do the same with 234 x 8 and 234 x 800. Each time, say out loud how many zeros will follow before a single one is written.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many zeros are printed in the multiplier? Second rung, the phase's: where do those zeros go once the short fact has been worked? Third rung: the rail is cut to a two digit number multiplied by ten, and the child opens that single place by hand. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the short fact is the piece that has just been worked, so its digits are the ones under the eye, and a zero already in the answer looks like a zero that has been accounted for.
wrong.move: counts the zeros already sitting in the short fact and writes those, instead of the zeros the multiplier carries.
wrong.screen: the multiplier is drawn on its own above the rail with its zeros ringed and counted out loud, and then that many empty places open under the right hand end of the short fact one at a time, each naming itself as it opens. The child's answer stands beside the rail with the places it is short of left open and ringed, and neither number is cleared.

wrong.why: a number grows at its left hand end when it is written out, so the room that opens up for a bigger answer looks as though it belongs at the front of it.
wrong.move: opens the new places in front of the number instead of after it, so the zeros land at the leading end.
wrong.screen: the number is read out place by place with the zeros where the child put them, and then again with them at the other end, and the two readings are written one under the other along the rail with the place names lit under every digit of both. The leading zeros are heard naming nothing at all, and the child's reading is left standing.

phases.screen: the zeros rail with the number above it and empty places opening to its right
phases.soWhat: Use the short fact first, then write as many zeros as the multiplier carries.
phases.concept: Zeros at the end do the work for you

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, the first time a number is sent along the zeros rail. The digits do not jump and nothing is redrawn. One empty place opens under the right hand end of the number and the whole number slides one place to the left into it, with the place names lighting under each digit as they pass, ones becoming tens, tens becoming hundreds, all the way along. Ask for a hundred and two places open and the same slide happens twice over. Send the number back and the places close one at a time and the digits walk home. The same cards are worth hundreds in one position and hundreds of thousands three positions along, and not one of them was ever rewritten.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase one long number lies in the left tray with a one card and a zero card waiting on the corner of the bench beside it. On the second the same cards lie in both trays in two different arrangements and neither tray has been worked. On the third the expand and add strip stands open under the trays with a three digit multiplicand already broken into its hundreds, tens and ones and every small row beneath it empty. On the fourth the zeros rail runs along the foot of the bench with a number sitting above it and the places to its right still closed. The running count at the top left holds the arrangements worked against the arrangements standing on the bench, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the one card, or the right hand tray, or the first broken part, or the first closed place on the rail, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what the bench is going to do. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any cards in either tray, brackets anywhere, with the expand strip, the zeros rail and the pairing bay open alongside. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on multiplying by one and by zero, choosing the order, expanding a multiplicand and using the zeros of a round multiplier.
voiceLines: The same cards in both trays, arranged two different ways. Work them both.
Take the number once. Now take it no times at all. What came back each time?
Swap them over, then work both trays. Did the product move?
Break it into its places. Multiply each piece. Now put the pieces back together.
Say how many zeros will follow before you press. Then press and count them.
New cards on the bench. Choose the arrangement you would rather work.
Free play. Any cards, brackets anywhere, with the expand strip and the zeros rail open.
Put the cards back and let the trays work the two arrangements side by side.
You changed the arrangement every single time, and the product never moved.

observations.why: Changing the arrangement changes which multiplication is done first and how many rows it takes, and it leaves the answer exactly where it was.
observations.soWhat: The product is what a swap promises. The steps are not, so choose the arrangement you would rather write out.
observations.observe: Both trays landed on the same product, and the working drawn under the two of them did not look the same.

observations.why: Taking a number once is the number itself, and taking it no times at all is nothing, however many digits it had.
observations.soWhat: Neither of those two multipliers needs any working at all.
observations.observe: The one card handed the number straight back and the zero card emptied the tray, whatever length of number was in it.

observations.why: The hundreds, the tens and the ones are the number itself written apart, so taking each of them five times takes the whole number five times.
observations.soWhat: Breaking a multiplicand up before multiplying is allowed, and it makes every step small enough to hold in the head.
observations.observe: The parts of 625 broken up and multiplied came to 3000 and 100 and 25, and those add back to the same 3125 the whole number gave.

observations.why: Multiplying by ten, a hundred or a thousand moves every digit one, two or three places to the left, and the places left behind have to be held open by zeros.
observations.soWhat: Count the zeros the multiplier carries, not the zeros that happen to be sitting in the short fact you used.
observations.observe: On the rail the digits never changed. The only thing that changed was how many places had opened underneath them.

description: Two trays that hold the same numbers in different arrangements, a strip that breaks a number up before multiplying it, and a rail where zeros do the work.

source_tool.name: Shortcut Bench
source_tool.blurb: Two trays that hold the same numbers in different arrangements, a strip that breaks a number up before multiplying it, and a rail where zeros do the work.

serves.exercise: calculating the six given products mentally, by one, by ten and by multiples of ten
working the four products mentally, by a hundred, by two hundred, by ten and by a single digit
working out how many tablets ten strips of ten tablets hold

source_tool.description: The bench carries two trays side by side and one set of number cards that belongs to both. Cards dropped into the left tray can be dropped into the right in a different order, or with a different pair bracketed to go first, and both trays work at once so the two products land together and can be read against each other. A one card and a zero card sit in the corner and can be dropped into either tray at any time, which settles the two rules the chapter states before all the others. An expand and add strip opens beneath the trays: it splits a multiplicand into its hundreds, tens and ones, multiplies each part in its own small row, and adds the rows back, with the whole number worked beside it so the two totals can be compared. A zeros rail runs along the foot of the bench, where a number multiplied by ten, a hundred or a thousand keeps its digits and slides left over opening zeros, and a multiple such as sixty is handled as a short fact followed by its zeros. A pairing bay takes three cards and lights whichever two of them multiply to a round number, without saying which product is easiest until the child has chosen.
source_tool.art_direction: Two trays and a rail of zeros / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: ruled column mats with a heading over every column, digit cards that can be picked up and dropped, place cards that split off a multiplier, trays that hold a number while it is taken several times, a table strip that grows a row at a time, and a ruled grid with a diagonal in every cell.

A multiplication set out in columns always shows its columns: one digit to a column, every column under its named heading, the rows aligned by their right ends, and a horizontal rule between the last row and the product. A bare row of digits with no column mat behind it is never used to teach multiplying.
A carried digit is always drawn small, inside a ring above the column it is being added into, never in the margin and never below the rule.
A partial product row is drawn with the place of the multiplier that made it named beside it, and with its trailing zeros written rather than implied.

A lattice is drawn as a true grid of equal square cells with one straight diagonal in every cell, all running the same way, the digits of the two numbers sitting outside the grid, and every cell holding two digits on either side of its diagonal even when the pair multiplies to less than ten, so that nothing has to be carried while multiplying.
Where tokens or groups stand for a quantity, exactly the stated number of them is drawn, every group holds the same count, they never overlap, and they stay countable at a glance.
A column is told apart by its heading first and by its band second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a column, a cell or a token the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. The number being multiplied is deep blue, the number it is multiplied by is amber, and the product under the rule is green, and those three are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. A digit carried into the next column is vermilion, so it is told apart from the digits it is joining. A partial product row, made by one place of the multiplier, is rose, so a row is read as a part before it is read as an answer. A zero holding a place open, and a place of the multiplier that is skipped, are both grey, because neither one is a quantity. All of that holds in greyscale, because a carried digit is told apart by being small and sitting in a ring above its column before it is told apart by its colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Put the cards back and let the trays work the two arrangements side by side.
voice.onNext: New cards on the bench. Choose the arrangement you would rather work.
voice.opening: The same cards in both trays, arranged two different ways. Work them both.
voice.onFinish: You changed the arrangement every single time, and the product never moved.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any cards, brackets anywhere, with the expand strip and the zeros rail open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: One leaves it alone and zero flattens it
The order is yours to choose
A number can be broken up before it is multiplied
Zeros at the end do the work for you

placement.where: After one product has been worked twice on paper, once each way round, so the two answers are already known to match. The tool is what lets an arrangement be changed without the numbers being written out again.

answer_key.rule: Multiplying by one gives the number back, and multiplying by zero gives zero. The product does not change when the multiplicand and the multiplier are swapped, and it does not change however three or more numbers are grouped, so any arrangement may be chosen and the pair that makes a round number is the pair worth taking first. A multiplicand may be broken into its places, each place multiplied, and the parts added, and the total is the same as multiplying the whole number at once. Multiplying by ten, a hundred or a thousand writes one, two or three zeros after the number. For a multiple such as sixty or eight hundred, use the short fact first and then write the zeros the multiplier carries.
answer_key.wrong: Both trays work their products again side by side, and on the zeros rail the places open one at a time beneath the digits so the zeros can be counted as they arrive. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Multiplying by one takes the number once, so nothing changes and the answer is 4826.
Multiplying by zero takes the number no times at all.
Nothing taken no times is nothing, so 4826 x 0 = 0.
items.question: What is 4826 x 1, and what is 4826 x 0?
items.checkpoint: One hands the number back and zero flattens it, whatever the number is.
items.misconception: Writing 4826 for the product with zero, by treating zero the way one behaves.

steps: Swapping the multiplicand and the multiplier leaves the product alone, so 6 x 427 is the same as 427 x 6.
That way the long number sits on the mat and the single digit does the work.
Working the columns gives 2562, so 6 x 427 = 2562.
items.question: Find 6 x 427 by changing the order of the two numbers.
items.checkpoint: The order may be chosen, so arrange the two numbers whichever way is easier to work.
items.misconception: Believing the number written first must be the one that goes on the mat.

steps: 348 is 300 + 40 + 8, so each part is multiplied by 6 on its own.
items.question: Expand the multiplicand and find 348 x 6.
items.checkpoint: A number may be broken into its places, each place multiplied, and the parts added.
items.misconception: Multiplying only the hundreds part and forgetting that the tens and the ones still have to be taken.

steps: Multiplying by ten writes one zero after the number, giving 4730.
Multiplying by a hundred writes two zeros, giving 47,300.
For 4000, use the short fact 473 x 4 = 1892 and then write the three zeros the multiplier carries, giving 18,92,000.
items.question: Find 473 x 10, then 473 x 100, then 473 x 4000.
items.checkpoint: Use the short fact first, then write as many zeros as the multiplier carries.
items.misconception: Writing 1892 with only one zero after it, by counting the zeros of the short fact instead of the zeros of the multiplier.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Find 8 x 312 by putting the longer number on the mat first.
Find 372 x 5 x 20 by pairing two of the numbers first.
items.final_answer: 37,200, by multiplying 5 and 20 first to make 100

items.question: Expand the multiplicand and find 526 x 4.
Which of these is another way to find 48 x 9: (40 x 9) + (8 x 9), or (40 + 9) x (8 + 9)?
items.final_answer: (40 x 9) + (8 x 9), because it comes to 360 + 72 = 432, which is what 48 x 9 comes to

items.question: Find 264 x 700.
items.final_answer: 1,84,800, because 264 x 7 = 1848 and the multiplier carries two zeros

items.question: A strip holds 20 tablets and a carton holds 300 such strips. How many tablets are in the carton?
items.final_answer: 6000 tablets, because 2 x 3 = 6 and the two numbers carry three zeros between them

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: works the same cards as two products at once and stands the answers together
reverses the order of the cards in one tray
closes a bracket around a pair so that pair is multiplied first
drops a one or a zero into either tray and shows what it does to the product
splits the multiplicand into its places, multiplies each and adds the rows back
slides the digits left over opening zeros for ten, a hundred, a thousand and their multiples
lights whichever two of three cards multiply to a round number

teaching_notes: Show each rule before naming it, the way the page does. Multiply something by one and then by zero and let the class say what happened before the sentence is read out. For the expand strip, work the chapter's own example first: 625 x 5 is 600 x 5 + 20 x 5 + 5 x 5, which is 3000 + 100 + 25, and it comes to 3125 whichever way it is worked. Then the zeros rail, and here make them say how many zeros will follow before they press, because counting the zeros of the multiplier is the whole skill and counting the zeros of the short fact is the whole mistake. The money example on the same page is the best argument for the rail: fifty notes of a hundred rupees and twenty-five notes of ten rupees come to 5000 and 250, which is Rs 5250, and nobody counted a single note. Leave the pairing bay until last. Three numbers to multiply and a free choice of which two go first is a real decision, and a child who has made it once stops working strictly from the left every time.
generation_prompt: Build a multiplication properties tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. Two trays side by side share one set of number cards, and both trays work their products at once so their answers land together for comparison. A swap control reverses the cards in a tray, and on a three card tray brackets close around any pair so that pair is multiplied first and held as a single card. A one card and a zero card sit in the corner and can be dropped into either tray, with the tray handing the number straight back for one and collapsing visibly to nothing for zero. An expand and add strip opens under the trays, splitting the multiplicand into its hundreds, tens and ones, multiplying each in its own small row and adding the rows back, with the whole number worked alongside for comparison. A zeros rail along the foot holds the number with empty places opening to its right: multiplying by ten, a hundred or a thousand slides the digits left over one, two or three opening zeros with the place names lit as they fill, and a multiple such as sixty or eight hundred works the short fact first and then opens its zeros. A pairing bay takes three cards and, once the child has chosen, lights whichever two multiply to a round number. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Put the same numbers in both trays in different arrangements and work them both. Bracket whichever pair is easiest and multiply that pair first. Open the expand strip and break the long number into its places before you multiply it. On the zeros rail, say how many zeros will follow before you press.
